title: The standby generator, up close
alt: A section through a standby generator in its sound-dampened enclosure in the yard. Outside air comes in through louvres at one end, drawn as blue lines; a diesel engine turns the alternator, which sends power out in a cable to the switchgear; a fan pushes the air through the radiator and out the far end, drawn as red lines. Fuel comes from a belly tank under the engine, filled at a fill point. Exhaust leaves through a silencer and a stack. Engine noise spreads as rings across the lot line to the neighbour's house. A clock shows the monthly test run.
sources: About 78 dB(A) at 7 m for one set: Rehlko KD2000, sound level 2 (maker claim)
80 dB(A) limit where the sound is heard: City of Vancouver Noise By-law, as used by the tool's noise card
At least 12 hours of fuel on site: Uptime Institute (Heslin 2014), industry guidance
Monthly test: 60 minutes at 30 % of rated load or more: CSA C282 as summarised by a fire department (secondary summary of a licensed standard; whether IT standby sets fall under it is open)
drawn_generically: the enclosure, engine, alternator, fan, radiator, belly tank, fill point, silencer and stack: a generic diesel genset, not the specific model in the layouts

steps.caption: The standby generator waits in the yard, inside a sound-dampened enclosure. It only runs when the grid fails, or for a test.
Inside, a diesel engine turns an alternator, which makes the electricity. Air comes in at one end; a fan pushes it through the radiator and out the other end, hot.
Fuel is stored in a belly tank under the engine, filled from a fill point at the side. Sites keep at least 12 hours of fuel.
Exhaust leaves through a silencer and a stack above the enclosure.
Engine noise spreads across the yard and the lot line to the neighbours.
Once a month it runs for a test, for an hour at 30 % of its load or more, so it is ready when the grid fails.
